input_representation_sections.heading: 2.1 Overview of GEM-GPT
input_representation_sections.text:
The overall architecture of GEM-GPT is shown in Fig. 1. GEM-GPT uses a GPTbased autoregressive architecture to generate SMILES strings conditioned on a desired transcriptional transition from a diseased cell state toward its healthy counterpart (Fig. 1a). During generation, a pretrained and frozen scRNA-seq foundation model encodes the paired diseased and healthy gene expression profiles into layer-specific transcriptomic representations. In this study, we use scGPT [18] because its celllevel embeddings capture cell type information directly from transcriptomic profiles and generalize across diverse single-cell datasets, enabling cell type-specific molecular generation without requiring explicit cell type annotations as input. The cell-state embedding derived from scGPT serves as the initial token embedding for molecular generation, providing explicit cell type-specific conditioning from the beginning of the autoregressive process.

Fig. 1b presents the detailed architecture of each GEM-GPT block. To effectively integrate transcriptomic and molecular information, we introduce a deep fused attention mechanism that couples the molecular hidden state with the corresponding scGPT hidden representations at every layer of GEM-GPT. Specifically, the molecular representation is separately fused with the scGPT representations of the diseased and healthy cell states. The difference between the resulting conditioned molecular representations is then propagated to the next GEM-GPT layer, allowing the desired disease-to-healthy transcriptional shift to guide each stage of molecular generation. This layer-by-layer integration incorporates transcriptomic information throughout the entire generation process, rather than only at the input level, and enables direct and repeated interactions between cellular-state and molecular representations.

GEM-GPT was compared with state-of-the-art transcriptomics-guided molecular generation baselines, including MolGAN [13], GxVAEs [14], GexMolGen [15], and MolGene-E [16]. We first evaluated whether GEM-GPT could generate hit-like molecules from compound-induced gene expression profiles in both seen and previously unseen cell lines. We then examined whether GEM-GPT could generalize across perturbation modalities by generating pharmacologically relevant molecules from CRISPR knock-out transcriptomic signatures. Finally, we applied GEM-GPT to single-cell transcriptomic profiles from patients with Opioid Use Disorder to identify personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic candidates, including molecules with distinct chemotypes and repurposable FDA-approved drugs. Together, these experiments evaluate the ability of GEM-GPT to learn generalizable transcriptometo-molecule relationships and support personalized, cell type-specific therapeutic design.

heading_path: 4.2.3 Personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic design for OUD
input_representation_sections.heading: 4.2.3 Personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic design for OUD
input_representation_sections.text:
We applied GEM-GPT to single-cell transcriptomic profiles from patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) to evaluate personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic generation. The single-cell RNA-seq dataset was obtained by [29] and included patientderived and healthy samples. The analysis focused on the 4 brain cell types covered in the dataset: astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes (ODC), and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPC).

For each patient and cell type, gene expression profiles were aggregated across cells using pseudobulk averaging. A healthy reference profile was constructed from all healthy individuals' cells of the same cell type. GEM-GPT generated up to 1,000 molecular candidates for each pair of profiles. GxVAEs [14], which is the bestperforming baseline in our other experiments, was evaluated using the same inputs and generation scale. All generated SMILES strings were processed using the same RDKit-based validity, sanitization, and canonicalization procedure.

Cell type-specific molecular generation was examined by comparing molecular sets generated for different cell types or the same cell type within the same patient. Random splitting was repeated five times to reduce variation caused by a single partition.

input_representation_sections.heading: 1 Introduction
input_representation_sections.text:
Drug discovery and development are among the most resource-intensive and high-risk endeavors in biomedical science. A new drug requires on average 10-15 years and over $ 1-2 billion to progress from initial concept to regulatory approval [1]. Despite substantial investment in target identification, lead optimization, and preclinical validation, approximately 90% of drug candidates that enter clinical trials ultimately fail [1, 2]. A major contributor to this high failure rate is the continued reliance on the onedrug-one-target paradigm in modern drug discovery [3, 4]. Although this approach has yielded important breakthroughs, particularly in oncology where actionable mutations drive targeted therapies [5], it fundamentally oversimplifies the complexity of most human diseases [6]. Chronic and systemic conditions such as neurological disorders, autoimmune diseases, metabolic syndromes, and substance use disorders are inherently polygenic, multifactorial, and dependent on cellular and physiological context [3, 4]. In such diseases, modulation of a single molecular node rarely restores homeostasis across the broader biological network, which may contribute to the particularly high attrition rates observed in these therapeutic areas [7]. Systems pharmacology and network-based drug discovery have emerged as alternative frameworks that emphasize the coordinated modulation of disease-relevant biological networks rather than isolated molecular targets [3, 6]. Yet despite their conceptual and therapeutic potential, relatively few AI-driven computational tools have been developed to implement these principles systematically and at scale, particularly for the de novo design of novel therapeutic compounds.

Acomplementary and increasingly important goal in drug discovery is the design of therapies tailored to the individual patient. Inter-individual variability in disease biology, which arises from genetic background, epigenetic state, environmental exposures, and tissue-specific gene expression, means that population-level measures of drug response may obscure substantial differences in treatment efficacy and safety [8, 9]. The past decade has witnessed the rise of precision medicine, wherein patient-specific molecular profiles guide therapeutic decision-making [9]. However, precision drug design, defined here as the de novo generation of molecules tailored to a patient's specific molecular disease state, remains an unmet challenge. This limitation arises partly because conventional target-based approaches generally do not incorporate the cellular and transcriptomic context that distinguishes individual patients, and partly because computational frameworks capable of integrating patient-specific omics data with generative molecular design in a scalable manner remain limited.

The advent of transcriptomics and, more recently, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has substantially expanded our ability to characterize disease processes at cellular resolution. By profiling the gene expression of thousands of individual cells simultaneously, scRNA-seq reveals cell type-specific transcriptional programs that are invisible to bulk sequencing approaches, enabling identification of novel disease-relevant cell subpopulations, drug targets, and biomarkers [10]. This cellular resolution is particularly critical for studying heterogeneous diseases, in which distinct cell populations may exhibit different pathological states and responses to therapeutic perturbations [10]. The use of scRNA-seq for personalized and cell type-specific drug discovery, in which therapeutic molecules are designed to shift disease-associated cellular states toward healthy states, provides an alternative to conventional target-centric drug discovery [11, 12]. Because this approach does not require prior identification of a specific molecular target, it is particularly applicable to diseases with complex or incompletely understood molecular mechanisms, including many chronic and systemic conditions [11, 12]. Nevertheless, compared with target-based drug discovery, relatively few computational methods have been developed for systems pharmacology approaches centered on the modulation of cellular states [13-16], and the integration of single-cell transcriptomics with de novo molecular generation remains a largely open problem [16].

The emergence of foundation models pretrained on large-scale biological data has provided new computational tools for addressing this challenge. scRNA-seq foundation models [17, 18] have demonstrated the capacity to learn rich, generalizable representations of gene regulatory networks and cellular states through self-supervised learning, enabling strong transfer performance across a range of downstream biological tasks. In parallel, generative models for molecular design have advanced rapidly. Variational autoencoders [19], generative adversarial networks [20], transformer-based chemical language models [21, 22], and equivariant diffusion models [23] have each demonstrated the capacity to generate novel, drug-like molecules with desired physicochemical and biological properties, greatly accelerating the exploration of chemical space relative to traditional high-throughput screening [24]. Several recent works have begun to bridge transcriptomics and molecular generation. MolGAN [13] pioneered this direction by conditioning a generative adversarial network on bulk transcriptomic signatures to generate hit-like molecules with desired gene expression effects, demonstrating the feasibility of phenotype-guided molecular design. GxVAEs [14] extended this concept by employing two jointly trained variational autoencoders, one to extract latent features from bulk gene expression profiles and another to generate drug-like molecules conditioned on those features. GexMolGen [15] further advanced the field by adopting a cross-modal 'first-align-then-generate' strategy that leverages a scRNA-seq foundation model (specifically scGPT) to encode bulk gene expression signatures and align them with a scaffold-based molecular decoder, yielding hit-like molecules with improved structural similarity to known active compounds. Most recently, MolGeneE [16] made a critical step toward single-cell resolution by combining a cross-modal domain adaptation model to harmonize bulk and single-cell chemical transcriptomics data with a contrastive learning-based generative model, demonstrating that single-cell omics data can, in principle, guide molecular generation.

Despite these advances, existing transcriptomics-guided molecular generation methods retain several important limitations. First, MolGAN and GxVAEs rely exclusively on bulk transcriptomics data, primarily the L1000 database, which lacks the cellular resolution needed to distinguish disease-associated states across individual cell types and therefore limits the generation of molecules tailored to specific cell populations within a patient. Second, GexMolGen and MolGene-E employ two-stage frameworks in which transcriptomic and molecular representations are learned separately and subsequently aligned through contrastive learning. Because the integration of the two modalities is primarily achieved through representation alignment rather than continuous interaction throughout molecular generation, these approaches may be limited in their ability to capture cell-state-dependent chemical-gene relationships. Third, existing methods are not explicitly designed to preserve cell type-specific transcriptomic differences during molecular generation and have not systematically demonstrated that distinct cellular states lead to correspondingly distinct molecular outputs. Finally, none of these approaches has been evaluated for personalized drug discovery in patient-derived cohorts, nor have they demonstrated robust generalization to previously unseen cell types. These capabilities are important for extending transcriptomics-guided molecular generation to heterogeneous diseases and clinically relevant settings.

Given these limitations, none of these methods have been applied to single cellbased drug discovery. Opioid use disorder (OUD) provides a clinically important example of the need for personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic design. The ongoing opioid epidemic remains a major public health crisis, yet pharmacological treatment options for OUD remain limited, and relapse and inadequate treatment response are common [25]. Emerging single-cell transcriptomic studies have revealed that opioid exposure induces heterogeneous transcriptional changes across distinct neuronal and glial cell populations within brain reward circuits, and that these responses vary substantially across patients [26, 27]. This heterogeneity at both the patient and cell type levels suggests that uniform pharmacological strategies may not adequately address the diverse molecular states associated with OUD. Personalized therapeutic design based on individual, cell type-specific transcriptomic profiles may therefore provide a more direct approach for identifying compounds capable of modulating disease-associated cellular states.

Here we introduce GEM-GPT ( G ene E xpression-guided M olecular G enerative P re-trained T ransformer), a single cell transcriptomics-guided molecular generation framework designed to address these limitations through three main contributions. First, GEM-GPT employs a biology-inspired deep fusion strategy that integrates scRNA-seq foundation model representations with molecular token representations at each hidden layer of a unified generative architecture. This design enables continuous interaction between cellular-state and molecular representations during generation, supporting more detailed modeling of cell-state-dependent chemical-gene relationships than alignment-based approaches. Second, by conditioning molecular generation directly on cell type-aware disease-state representations derived from a pretrained single cell foundation model, GEM-GPT generates personalized and cell type-specific candidate molecules predicted to shift disease-associated transcriptional states toward healthy phenotypes. It produces distinct molecular outputs across cell types, generalizes to previously unseen cell types, and consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines across multiple evaluation settings. Third, through its application to OUD, GEM-GPT identifies diverse candidate molecules targeting cell type-specific disease states in individual patients, including FDA-approved drugs relevant to OUD, establishing a new paradigm for AI-driven, omics-based, personalized drug discovery.

Fig. 1 Overview of GEM-GPT. a. GEM-GPT autoregressively generates molecular SMILES strings by conditioning on the transcriptional transition from a diseased cell state toward its healthy counterpart. A pretrained scRNA-seq foundation model, scGPT, encodes the diseased and healthy gene expression profiles, while the scGPT-derived cell-state embedding serves as the initial token embedding for cell type-specific molecular generation. b. Detailed architecture of a GEM-GPT block and the proposed deep fused attention mechanism. At each layer, the molecular hidden state is separately fused with the corresponding scGPT hidden representations of the healthy and diseased cell states. The difference between the resulting conditioned molecular representations is propagated to the next GEM-GPT layer, allowing the desired disease-to-healthy transcriptional shift to guide molecular generation throughout the network. The enlarged view illustrates the layer-level interaction between the trainable molecular attention module and the frozen scGPT attention module through concatenated key and value representations.

sections_for_screening.text:
2 Results
2.4 GEM-GPT generates personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic candidates for OUD using patient and healthy single-cell transcriptomic profiles
Having established that GEM-GPT can generalize across compounds, cell lines, and perturbation modalities, we next investigated whether it could support personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic design for a complex disease characterized by substantial inter-individual and cellular heterogeneity. We applied GEM-GPT to single-cell RNA-sequencing profiles obtained from individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD) and healthy individuals [29], focusing on four brain cell types: astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes (ODC), and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPC). None of these cell types was represented in the L1000 training set, making this application a stringent evaluation of molecular generation from previously unseen cellular populations.
For each cell type, a healthy reference gene expression profile was constructed by averaging the corresponding single-cell profiles from healthy individuals, whereas a patient-specific OUD expression profile was constructed separately for each OUD patient using cells of the same annotated cell type. Each model input therefore consisted of a paired patient-specific OUD profile and a cell type-matched healthy reference profile. GEM-GPT conditioned molecular generation on the transcriptional transition from the patient-specific OUD state toward the corresponding healthy state, thereby producing candidate molecules specific to both the individual patient and cell type. The generated molecules were subsequently analyzed using the Similarity Ensemble Approach (SEA) [30] to search their potential protein targets. The resulting targets associated with OUD were then used to prioritize candidate molecules, connecting patient- and cell type-specific molecular generation with disease-relevant target networks (Fig. 4a).
To determine whether the generated chemical space reflected inter-patient heterogeneity, valid molecules were represented using Morgan fingerprints and grouped into 30 molecular clusters. For each patient and cell type, we calculated the proportion of generated molecules assigned to each cluster. Because each molecular set was generated from a paired patient-specific OUD profile and cell type-matched healthy reference profile, differences in the resulting chemical space reflect differences in the disease-to-healthy transcriptional transitions across patients. The resulting heatmaps showed distinct molecular cluster distributions among patients within the same cell type (Fig. 4b). Different patients exhibited enrichment in different clusters and distinct combinations of molecular patterns, indicating that GEM-GPT did not generate a uniform candidate distribution across the patient cohort. These patient-dependent molecular distributions demonstrate that GEM-GPT translates inter-patient heterogeneity in OUD-associated transcriptional states into personalized candidate chemical spaces.

Fig. 4 GEM-GPT enables personalized and cell type-specific therapeutic design for OUD. a. Pipeline for generating candidate molecules from paired cell type-specific gene expression profiles of OUD patients and healthy individuals, followed by SEA-based search of OUD-related targets. b. Molecular cluster distributions of generated candidates across all OUD patients for astrocytes, microglia, ODC, and OPC. Differences in cluster distributions among patients within the same cell type indicate personalized molecular generation. c. Mean Jaccard overlap between molecular sets generated within the same cell type and across different cell types. ∆ denotes the within-celltype minus cross-cell-type overlap. GEM-GPT exhibited a substantially larger separation between the two conditions than GxVAEs, supporting stronger cell type-specific differentiation of the generated molecular sets. d. FDA-approved compounds absent from the training set identified among GEM-GPT-generated candidates associated with OUD-related targets through SEA-based target prediction, including naltrexone, naloxone, and clonidine.

<!-- image -->

We next evaluated whether GEM-GPT generated distinct molecular candidates for different cell types within the same patient. For each patient, we compared the Jaccard overlap between molecular sets generated from independent subsets of the same cell type with the overlap between molecular sets generated from different cell types. GxVAEs showed similar within-cell-type and cross-cell-type overlaps, with mean values of 0.055 and 0.054, respectively, resulting in only a minimal separation of ∆ = 0 . 001 (Fig. 4c). This pattern suggests that GxVAEs generated largely shared molecular sets across different cell types. In contrast, GEM-GPT showed a mean within-cell-type overlap of 0.044 and a substantially lower cross-cell-type overlap of 0.014, resulting in a markedly larger separation of ∆ = 0 . 030. The lower molecular overlap across cell types relative to that within the same cell type demonstrates that GEM-GPT responds to cell type-specific transcriptional states and generates distinct therapeutic candidate spaces for different cell types within individual OUD patients.

Finally, SEA-based target analysis identified generated candidates predicted to interact with OUD-related targets. Among these candidates, GEM-GPT identified 3 FDA-approved compounds related to OUD that were absent from the training set: naltrexone, naloxone, and clonidine (Fig. 4d). In contrast, GxVAE did not recover any FDA-approved drugs relevant to OUD under the same analysis. The generation of clinically relevant compounds without prior exposure during training suggests that GEM-GPT learned transferable relationships between transcriptional disease states and pharmacologically relevant chemical structures rather than simply memorizing known drugs. Together, these results demonstrate that GEM-GPT can translate patient- and cell type-level transcriptional heterogeneity into differentiated molecular candidate spaces while identifying clinically relevant FDA-approved drugs, providing a proof of concept for personalized systems pharmacology in OUD.

sections_for_screening.text:
4 Methods
4.1 GEM-GPT
4.1.2 Autoregressive molecular generation and model training
Molecules are represented as SMILES strings and tokenized using the character-level vocabulary. Each sequence is surrounded by beginning-of-sequence and end-ofsequence tokens and is padded to a maximum sequence length of 80 tokens.
During training, GEM-GPT receives paired control and compound-perturbed expression profiles together with the SMILES representation of the perturbing compound. The perturbed profile is treated as the state induced by the reference molecule, while the corresponding control profile represents the cellular state before perturbation. The model is trained to predict each SMILES token conditioned on the preceding molecular tokens and the paired transcriptional states.
The training objective is the autoregressive negative log-likelihood:
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->
Only the molecular generator and deep fused attention modules are updated during optimization. The pretrained scGPT parameters remain frozen. The model is optimized using the AdamW optimizer. The checkpoint with the lowest validation loss is selected for molecular generation.
During inference, molecules are generated autoregressively using beam search. Generation terminates when the end-of-sequence token is produced or when the maximum sequence length is reached. The generated sequences are decoded into SMILES strings and processed using RDKit. SMILES strings that cannot be parsed or sanitized are treated as invalid. Valid molecules are converted to canonical SMILES for downstream analyses.

heading_path: Evaluating the utilities of foundation models in single-cell data analysis
primary_data_source_chunk.heading: Abstract
primary_data_source_chunk.text:
Evaluating the utilities of foundation models in single-cell data analysis
Abstract
Foundation Models (FMs) have made significant strides in both industrial and scientific domains. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of FMs for single-cell sequencing data analysis through comprehensive experiments across eight downstream tasks pertinent to single-cell data. Overall, the top FMs include scGPT, Geneformer, and CellPLM by considering model performances and user accessibility among ten single-cell FMs. However, by comparing these FMs with task-specific methods, we found that single-cell FMs may not consistently excel than task-specific methods in all tasks, which challenges the necessity of developing foundation models for single-cell analysis. In addition, we evaluated the effects of hyper-parameters, initial settings, and stability for training single-cell FMs based on a proposed scEval framework, and provide guidelines for pre-training and fine-tuning, to enhance the performances of single-cell FMs. Our work summarizes the current state of single-cell FMs, points to their constraints and avenues for future development, and offers a freely available evaluation pipeline to benchmark new models and improve method development.

It primarily signifies the distribution disparity in scRNA-seq datasets originating from the same tissue, which can be attributed to various factors [110]. Since most of the single-cell FMs choose to reconstruct the masked gene expression levels in the pre-training stage, we can use an encoder-decoder structure (similar to an auto-encoder [118]) as well as extra fine-tuning blocks to unify their architectures. Moreover, we split the eight tasks into two types. For tasks included in sub-task 1, we need an extra fine-tuning block to generate the results. Each FM has its specific running settings, and their default modes can be classified into fine-tuning-based models and zero-shot-learning-based models, thus we propose a framework focusing on the outputs of different single-cell FMs to unify the evaluation process. To analyze the factors affecting single-cell FMs, we also adjusted the factors of different FMs and collected their results for evaluation. Moreover, scEval contains different evaluation pipelines for different tasks, and it can also be easily extended to evaluate more tasks by adding more functions.

Our third goal is to assess other abilities of single-cell FMs, including: 1. zero-shot learning; 2. model scaling [75, 96, 252]; 3. cross-species data analysis; 4. biological mechanism exploration; and 5. stability.

Parameters and tasks. Most single-cell FMs share the pre-training process. By considering the overlap among various single-cell FMs, we have selected scGPT, scBERT, and Geneformer as representative examples for our analysis. We also highlight the downstream tasks in Figure 1.1 (a). We focus on eight fine-tuning tasks in total: 1. Batch Effect Correction; 2. Multi-omic Data Integration; 3. Cell-type Annotation; 4. Gene Function Prediction; 5. Perturbation Prediction; 6. Gene Network Analysis; 7. Imputation; and 8. scRNA-seq Simulation. By compiling all the hyper-parameters across different models, we present a list of factors that can affect the model performance categorized by types in Figure 1.1 (b). The definition of different hyper-parameters is discussed in original appendix. To analyze the effect of different hyper-parameters, initial settings, and optimizers, we selected representative datasets for different tasks. For Batch Effect Correction and Cell-type Annotation, we selected Pancrm, HumanPBMC, Cell Lines, and MCA because they cover various data types. Pancrm is from Pancreas tissue and has five batches. HumanPBMC is from PBMC and has nine cell types. Cell Lines has two cell types, as a binary label dataset. MCA is from Mus musculus . For Multi-omic Data Integration, we included all of the four datasets we used to analyze because their scales cover a large range. For Gene Function Prediction, we included all of the three datasets we used to analyze because they correspond to different sub-tasks. For Perturbation Prediction, we included all of the three datasets we used to analyze because their scales cover a large range and are from different sources.

It primarily signifies the distribution disparity in scRNA-seq datasets originating from the same tissue, which can be attributed to various factors [110]. Multi-omic Data Integration. Multi-omic Data Integration is a key step for multi-omic data analysis [197]. It is akin to an advanced form of batch effect correction. If unpaired multi-omic data are present, the objective is to map different datasets into a shared space for subsequent analysis. If paired multi-omic data are present, the goal is to assess whether the use of multi-omic data can contribute to learning a more comprehensive representation of the data. A significant challenge here is how to align omics at the feature level. For instance, the feature of the scRNAseq data is a gene, the feature of the scATAC-seq data is a peak, and the feature of the protein data is a protein. The tokenization step can become complex given different modalities. We treat this task as a data integration problem. We used the same metrics for multi-omic data integration as those for Batch Effect Correction.

Cell-type Annotation. Cell-type Annotation is another key step following single-cell data pre-processing [82]. This step annotates each cell with its accurate cell-type label, which can be achieved through prior knowledge [166] or computational methods [165]. These annotated cell-type labels can provide essential biological information for further downstream analysis, such as cell-type specific network analysis. In addition, drug response prediction [70] or single-cell disease classification [167] can also be treated as a variation of this task. A common approach employed by single-cell FMs in dealing with the cell-type annotation task is to use single-cell datasets for model training and treat the unannotated datasets as testing datasets. The challenge lies in predicting or annotating a set of cells that originate from studies different from the training datasets. Differently, SCimilarity pre-trained the model with cell-type labels to allow query of cell types directly for testing datasets. Moreover, the existence of cells with novel cell types (which are not included in the training datasets) further complicates the problem. We treat this task as a multi-label classification problem. Gene Function Prediction. Gene Function Prediction is important to identify the properties of genes across different conditions [205]. There are approximately 20,000 protein-encoding genes for humans [177] and only some are annotated with functions. Accurate prediction of gene function can help us understand and infer the role of genes in biological systems. Here we consider three types of functions for genes. The first one is dosage-sensitive or non-sensitive. Some genes are dosagesensitive, which means that they are significant in the analysis of Copy Number Variants (CNVs) related to genetic diagnosis. The second one is Bivalent versus nonmethylated. Bivalent chromatin structure is important to identify key developmental genes in embryonic stem cells (ESCs). Therefore, identifying bivalently marked genes versus unmethylated genes is important. The third one is Bivalent versus Lys4-only methylated. Lys4-only-methylated genes are also different from bivalently marked genes. We compare the model output with the true gene labels. We treat this task as a binary classification problem. Here we used the same metrics as the cell-type annotation task. We used a public dataset [205] considering only labeled genes in the dataset for prediction and evaluation.

Perturbation Prediction. Perturbation Prediction [169] is a task based on gene editing and single-cell sequencing technologies. After silencing some genes, we can obtain unperturbed and perturbed gene expression levels by sequencing, which allows us to explore the interactions between genes. A well-known technique is Perturb-seq [47]. In perturbation prediction, we intend to predict the gene expression level after gene editing. Here a model may predict seen gene perturbation in the testing datasets (an easier one) or predict unseen gene perturbation in the testing datasets (a more difficult one). We treat this task as a regression problem. The metric we used here is MPC, and the details can be found in original appendix.3. In the perturbation prediction task, we construct the paired input-target datasets by selecting the cells with non-control guide identity and then randomly sample cells under the control condition, and then combine them as the training and testing datasets. Our Perturb-seq datasets are from GEARS [169], which contain cells with three conditions: control; one gene perturbation; and two genes perturbation. In the evaluation process, we combined case 2 and case 3. We also compared the MPC across all genes to avoid bias in the gene selection process.

Imputation. Imputation is a filling task related to missing data. Generally, we have two targets: 1. Perform imputation for scRNA-seq data to reduce data noise and fill in technical zeros with biologically meaningful values [77, 114]. 2. Perform imputation for spatial transcriptomic data because of unseen or unmeasured genes [11, 113]. According to [140], current spatial imputation methods do not show strong performance across different datasets. Using single-cell FMs, we can either use zero-shot learning to impute the unseen genes, or fine-tune our model based on reference scRNA-seq with more genes to perform imputation. We treat this task as a matrix-completion problem. Details of the metrics we used here can be found

Gene Network Analysis. Gene Network Analysis is a downstream task for single-cell datasets [72]. The objective is to infer specific gene networks (for example, Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) or Gene Co-expression Network (GCN)) from different datasets. A GRN can assist in understanding the regulatory relationships between genes and predicted perturbation outcomes. The challenge in this task stems from the Granger causal relationship or time-dependent correlation [44]. A GCN can be used to analyze genes with similar functions or uncover the characteristics of genes in some diseases [199]. This limitation means that we cannot determine which genes are the 'causes' of expression level changes in other genes only based on embeddings similarity or correlation. We treat this task as a network inference problem. In the gene network analysis task, we considered using the overlap between ground truth genes in certain pathways and inferred genes as one metric, and using the ratio of significant pathways related to inferred genes as the other metric. Details can be found in original appendix.4.

By arranging different sequences of masking genes or altering different seeds, we can generate new simulated scRNA-seq datasets from real ones. By modifying scGPT, we fine-tuned the baseline model based on the reference scRNA-seq dataset with reconstruction loss and utilized the outputs of the decoder part to generate the simulation datasets. Such simulation datasets do not have exactly the same gene expression profiles compared with the reference scRNA-seq dataset, but they should preserve the biological variation information from the reference dataset. We utilized scGPT to simulate datasets with batch effect or without batch effect. To simulate datasets with batch effect, we removed the loss function for removing batch effect in the original pipeline. To simulate datasets without batch effect, we kept the original pipeline for the batch effect correction task but utilized the outputs of the decoder rather than the encoder. We treat this task as a data-generation problem.

Simulation. scRNA-seq Simulation is a data generation task. Leveraging the generative pre-training process of scGPT, we can generate gene expressions based on real datasets. Since a prevalent issue with scRNA-seq data simulation is the considerable divergence between simulation datasets and real datasets [248], direct generation from real datasets is preferred.

We used the same metrics as Batch Effect Correction for evaluation. It is possible to produce diverse reconstruction outcomes from a single real dataset by varying the random seeds. This feature enables us to create simulated single-cell datasets. Notably, these generated datasets retain the same gene sets as their input counterparts. We generate the simulation results by multiplying the output of the gene expression decoder and Bernoulli decoder. We have the flexibility to generate datasets either with or without batch effects. If we intend to produce datasets with batch effects, the gradient reverse loss function is omitted. Conversely, to generate datasets without batch effects, we either retain this function or utilize single-batch data.

We retain the task-specific loss in the fine-tuning process as the baseline condition (All remove). Task-specific fine-tuning process. For the experiments we have in the Results section, we load the pre-training weights based on the requirement of different singlecell FMs. The pre-training weights we used can be found in our GitHub folder. After the fine-tuning process, we recorded the related metrics and conducted more analysis. In the experiments for all tasks, we chose scGPT as a baseline and representative model for the following three reasons. Firstly, scGPT is an open-source single-cell FM with the largest datasets for pre-training, and it is well-defined with detailed tutorials.

In addition, the architecture of scGPT is easy to adjust and includes multiple loss function components. The functions of Gene Function Prediction, Imputation, and Simulation for scGPT were designed in scEval for evaluation. The settings of hyperparameters for these tasks are transferred from the design for cell-type annotation and batch effect correction tasks. Moreover, different single-cell FMs have overlaps and unique terms in the pre-training and fine-tuning framework, but scGPT is the most general one. In each task, we also included task-specific methods as comparisons. Moreover, for Geneformer, scBERT, CellPLM, and CellLM, we also evaluated their performance based on shared hyper-parameters or optimizers with scGPT to verify if our rules found in scGPT can be extended for other single-cell FMs.

Statistical Analysis. scEval is an evaluation framework to benchmark the performances of scFMs across different tasks based on various datasets. In total, we consider eight tasks with 29 datasets. For data pre-processing, we refer modelspecific processing. All single-cell data are processed with Scanpy. Only Geneformer is processed by ranking the gene expression for generating cell and gene representations. For discrete data comparisons, we employed the Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test for paired data and the Mann-Whitney U test for unpaired data. For continuous data comparison, we utilize Pearson Correlation Coefficient to measure data similarity. The significance level for all hypothesis tests was set at 0.05.

heading_path: Evaluating the utilities of foundation models in single-cell data analysis
primary_data_source_section.heading: Abstract
primary_data_source_section.text: Foundation Models (FMs) have made significant strides in both industrial and scientific domains. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of FMs for single-cell sequencing data analysis through comprehensive experiments across eight downstream tasks pertinent to single-cell data. Overall, the top FMs include scGPT, Geneformer, and CellPLM by considering model performances and user accessibility among ten single-cell FMs. However, by comparing these FMs with task-specific methods, we found that single-cell FMs may not consistently excel than task-specific methods in all tasks, which challenges the necessity of developing foundation models for single-cell analysis. In addition, we evaluated the effects of hyper-parameters, initial settings, and stability for training single-cell FMs based on a proposed scEval framework, and provide guidelines for pre-training and fine-tuning, to enhance the performances of single-cell FMs. Our work summarizes the current state of single-cell FMs, points to their constraints and avenues for future development, and offers a freely available evaluation pipeline to benchmark new models and improve method development.

By arranging different sequences of masking genes or altering different seeds, we can generate new simulated scRNA-seq datasets from real ones. By modifying scGPT, we fine-tuned the baseline model based on the reference scRNA-seq dataset with reconstruction loss and utilized the outputs of the decoder part to generate the simulation datasets. Such simulation datasets do not have exactly the same gene expression profiles compared with the reference scRNA-seq dataset, but they should preserve the biological variation information from the reference dataset. We utilized scGPT to simulate datasets with batch effect or without batch effect. To simulate datasets with batch effect, we removed the loss function for removing batch effect in the original pipeline. To simulate datasets without batch effect, we kept the original pipeline for the batch effect correction task but utilized the outputs of the decoder rather than the encoder. We did not incorporate extra information for implementing this function. The quality of our simulation datasets can be evaluated by comparing them with the outputs of current simulation methods. We treat this task as a data-generation problem.

Simulation. scRNA-seq Simulation is a data generation task. Leveraging the generative pre-training process of scGPT, we can generate gene expressions based on real datasets. Since a prevalent issue with scRNA-seq data simulation is the considerable divergence between simulation datasets and real datasets [248], direct generation from real datasets is preferred.

We used the same metrics as Batch Effect Correction for evaluation. It is possible to produce diverse reconstruction outcomes from a single real dataset by varying the random seeds. This feature enables us to create simulated single-cell datasets. Notably, these generated datasets retain the same gene sets as their input counterparts. We generate the simulation results by multiplying the output of the gene expression decoder and Bernoulli decoder. We have the flexibility to generate datasets either with or without batch effects. If we intend to produce datasets with batch effects, the gradient reverse loss function is omitted. Conversely, to generate datasets without batch effects, we either retain this function or utilize single-batch data.

Ablation tests. Given that there is no existing work investigating the significance of different loss function components of single-cell FMs, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the impact of various loss function components. These include the Masked Gene Expression loss (Mask Loss), Zero Log Probability Loss (Prob Loss), Gene Expression Prediction for Cell Modelling Loss (GEPC Loss), and Elastic Cell Similarity Loss (ECS Loss). We retain the task-specific loss in the fine-tuning process as the baseline condition (All remove). Consequently, our null hypothesis ( H 0 ) is that the removal of the component C will not degrade the performance, while the alternative hypothesis ( H 1 ) is that the removal of component C will worsen the model's performance. Comparing the score after eliminating a specific component to the score from the default setting allows us to determine whether to reject the null hypothesis. The test we employed here includes both the paired Students' t-test and Wilcoxon Rank-sum test. The details of the different loss function components are shown below.

Model Scaling. [75, 96, 252] argue that due to the extensive number of parameters, FMs can manage specific tasks that small-scale models cannot handle. Such an attribute refers to the scaling law. We hypothesize that single-cell FMs may also possess this capability. To test this, we devise different scenarios similar to instances of model scaling to assess the performance of single-cell FMs. Such scenarios include: Cross-dataset Cell-type Annotation, Cross-species Cell-type Annotation, and Spatial Transcriptomic Data Analysis.

1. Mask Loss: In both pre-training and fine-tuning, we mask the expression levels of some genes, denoted as M mask , for gene expression prediction. The mask loss is motivated from this setting and works as follows,

Task-specific fine-tuning process. For the experiments we have in the Results section, we load the pre-training weights based on the requirement of different singlecell FMs. The pre-training weights we used can be found in our GitHub folder. After the fine-tuning process, we recorded the related metrics and conducted more analysis. In the experiments for all tasks, we chose scGPT as a baseline and representative model for the following three reasons. Firstly, scGPT is an open-source single-cell FM with the largest datasets for pre-training, and it is well-defined with detailed tutorials.

In addition, the architecture of scGPT is easy to adjust and includes multiple loss function components. The functions of Gene Function Prediction, Imputation, and Simulation for scGPT were designed in scEval for evaluation. The settings of hyperparameters for these tasks are transferred from the design for cell-type annotation and batch effect correction tasks. Moreover, different single-cell FMs have overlaps and unique terms in the pre-training and fine-tuning framework, but scGPT is the most general one. In each task, we also included task-specific methods as comparisons. Moreover, for Geneformer, scBERT, CellPLM, and CellLM, we also evaluated their performance based on shared hyper-parameters or optimizers with scGPT to verify if our rules found in scGPT can be extended for other single-cell FMs.

Statistical Analysis. scEval is an evaluation framework to benchmark the performances of scFMs across different tasks based on various datasets. In total, we consider eight tasks with 29 datasets. For data pre-processing, we refer modelspecific processing. All single-cell data are processed with Scanpy. Only Geneformer is processed by ranking the gene expression for generating cell and gene representations. For discrete data comparisons, we employed the Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test for paired data and the Mann-Whitney U test for unpaired data. For continuous data comparison, we utilize Pearson Correlation Coefficient to measure data similarity. The significance level for all hypothesis tests was set at 0.05.

heading_path: Evaluating the utilities of foundation models in single-cell data analysis
data_source_chunks.heading: Abstract
data_source_chunks.text:
Evaluating the utilities of foundation models in single-cell data analysis
Abstract
Foundation Models (FMs) have made significant strides in both industrial and scientific domains. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of FMs for single-cell sequencing data analysis through comprehensive experiments across eight downstream tasks pertinent to single-cell data. Overall, the top FMs include scGPT, Geneformer, and CellPLM by considering model performances and user accessibility among ten single-cell FMs. However, by comparing these FMs with task-specific methods, we found that single-cell FMs may not consistently excel than task-specific methods in all tasks, which challenges the necessity of developing foundation models for single-cell analysis. In addition, we evaluated the effects of hyper-parameters, initial settings, and stability for training single-cell FMs based on a proposed scEval framework, and provide guidelines for pre-training and fine-tuning, to enhance the performances of single-cell FMs. Our work summarizes the current state of single-cell FMs, points to their constraints and avenues for future development, and offers a freely available evaluation pipeline to benchmark new models and improve method development.

Leveraging Multi-Modal Foundation Models for Analyzing Spatial Multi-Omic and Histopathology Data
2.2 Results
Overview of spEMO. spEMO is an artificial intelligence system (AIS) for spatial multi-omic data analysis by integrating external knowledge as embeddings extracted from FMs. We support two different settings of spEMO, known as zero-shot embedding design and fine-tuning design. The former framework allows users to directly combine the embeddings from PFMs and LLMs for projecting spatial data into a new space, and the latter framework allows users to integrate embeddings with known methods to enhance their performances. The spot-level input images are computed by splitting the whole slide image into several patches with a pre-selected radius. We then embedded the patches with PFMs as spot-level embeddings. Furthermore, we define and perform several new tasks to demonstrate the power of multi-modal pathology analysis. The overall pipeline of spEMO is summarized in Figures 2.6.1 (a) and (b).
